glossary.agent: An AI system that can take steps and use tools to get a task done, not just answer questions.
glossary.on-prem: Software that runs on a company's own computers rather than being accessed as an online service.
glossary.ACL: Access Control List: a set of rules deciding who can view or change something.
glossary.knowledge graph: A way to organize information by showing how people, places, or things are connected.
glossary.computer vision: Software that examines pictures or video to spot and identify what's shown.
glossary.impressions: A count of how many times an ad could have been seen; it does not mean that many different people saw it.
glossary.virtual board replacement technology: A way to show viewers in different countries different ads on the boards around a sports field.
glossary.mindfulness: Paying attention to what's happening right now instead of letting the moment pass unnoticed.
glossary.BLT: A sandwich with bacon, lettuce, and tomato.
glossary.hedonic pleasure: Pleasure from things that feel good in the moment, like food or laughter.
glossary.Street View: A Google Maps feature that lets you look around streets using photos taken from the road.
glossary.anti-pattern: A common way of doing something that tends to cause problems.
glossary.pull request: A proposal to add your code changes to a shared project, usually asking others to review them first.
glossary.GitHub Actions: GitHub’s tool for running automatic tasks when things happen in a repository.
glossary.GitHub Pages: A GitHub service that publishes a website from files in a repository.
glossary.vendor lock-in: When relying on a company’s tools makes it difficult to move to another company’s tools.
glossary.version control: A way to keep a record of file changes so people can see or return to earlier versions.
glossary.Win32: Windows’ built-in tools for making desktop apps and their controls.
glossary.scroll bar thumb: The movable piece of a scroll bar that you drag to change your position.
glossary.context menu: A small menu that appears when you right-click.
glossary.Shift-click: Clicking while holding the Shift key; here, it jumps to the clicked spot.
glossary.Chromium: The browser project whose scroll bar Electron and other Web apps use.
glossary.plug-in hybrid: A car with a gas engine and a battery you can charge from an outlet, so it can drive on electricity too.
glossary.powertrain: The parts that move a car, such as its engine or electric motor.
glossary.platform: The shared base design and parts a carmaker uses to build different cars.
glossary.dual-motor: An electric-car setup with two motors instead of one.
glossary.max reasoning: A setting where an AI spends more effort working through a request before answering.
glossary.NSFW: Not Safe For Work: a warning that something may be awkward or unsuitable to view around coworkers.
glossary.GPS: Global Positioning System: satellites send signals that help devices work out where they are.
glossary.jamming: Sending interference that makes a signal difficult for a device to pick up.
glossary.electronic warfare: Using electronic signals to disrupt an opponent's equipment or protect your own.
glossary.inertial navigation: Working out direction and movement from onboard sensors instead of relying on satellite signals.
glossary.soft kill: A way to disable or confuse equipment without physically destroying it.
glossary.area denial: Making a place hard or risky for an opponent to use.
glossary.IDE: Integrated Development Environment: an app that brings coding and other development tools together.
glossary.semantic diff: A view of code changes that tries to show only the parts that matter, not every changed line.
glossary.AST-aware: Abstract Syntax Tree-aware: it compares how code is put together, not just the text characters.
glossary.LSP: Language Server Protocol: a common way for an editor to get language-specific help, such as code navigation.
glossary.WASM: WebAssembly: a way for an app to run plug-ins written in other programming languages.
glossary.agent trace: A record of what an AI agent did while working, which can help explain its choices.
glossary.Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index: A scorecard that combines results from several tests to compare AI models.
glossary.tokens: Small pieces of text an AI counts as it reads or writes; they can affect how much a request costs.
glossary.context window: The amount of text and information an AI can take into account at one time.
glossary.open weights: The model's learned settings are available for people to download and run themselves.
glossary.ground station: A place with antennas that links satellites to internet equipment on the ground.
glossary.modus operandi: The way someone carries out an act.
glossary.hybrid warfare: Using things like sabotage and disinformation to pressure or weaken another country.
glossary.Article 5: A NATO treaty rule saying an armed attack on one member is treated as an attack on all.
glossary.false flag: An attack staged to make it look like someone else did it.
glossary.Intelligence Index: A score used here to compare how well different AI models perform.
glossary.blended price: A combined price estimate based on a mix of input and output tokens.
glossary.value frontier: The models that aren't outscored by any cheaper option.
glossary.Z80: A kind of chip that runs instructions written for it.
glossary.REPL: Read-Eval-Print Loop: a prompt where you enter a command and see the result right away.
glossary.assembly language: A way of giving a chip simple, specific instructions using short words.
glossary.operand: A value or name that an instruction works with.
glossary.symbol: A name for a spot in a program, so you can refer to it by name instead of its location.
glossary.contrastive language model: An AI setup that compares an input with possible answers or actions to choose a close match.
glossary.frozen LLM: A large language model that's already trained and then left as-is while a smaller model learns to use its internal information.
glossary.hidden states: Information an AI builds as it processes input, which another model can use without seeing a written answer.
glossary.autoregressive (AR): Autoregressive: a way of producing text one piece at a time, with each new piece based on what came before.
glossary.agentic: Describes AI that chooses steps and acts toward a task, rather than only answering a question.
glossary.SIMD: Single Instruction, Multiple Data: a way to apply one operation to several values at once.
glossary.crate: A reusable package of Rust code that you can add to a project.
glossary.platform intrinsics: Functions that give your code access to a processor's specific built-in operations.
glossary.multiversioning: Keeping different versions of a function so a program can choose one that suits the machine it's running on.
glossary.unsafe code: Code Rust won't check for certain memory-safety mistakes automatically.
glossary.procedural macro: A Rust feature that writes or changes code when your program is being built.
glossary.FFT: Fast Fourier transform: a way to find which repeating frequencies make up a signal.
